diagnosis.hypothesis: A ~1.2s artificial database sleep (SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)) executed repeatedly in the inventory-service catalog (/products) query path inflates every catalog-dependent request by ~1200ms; the pricing module is unrelated and healthy.
diagnosis.root_cause: The inventory-service /products path executes a blocking SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) against Postgres on each catalog read. This is an injected/operational fault outside the application code: no `sleep` or pg_sleep call exists anywhere in allowlisted source (services/pricing.py, services/runtime.py, tests/pricing_contract.py), and pg_stat_statements shows pg_sleep executing ~53 times/second at a mean exec time of ~1202ms. Because runtime.py configures the async connection pool with timeout=0.8s, the ~1.2s statement also risks pool-connection timeouts and inflates inventory pool usage_ms (93840 vs single-digit-thousands for peers). Every gateway/order request that fans out to inventory /products inherits the ~1206ms; payment, user and notification hops remain single-digit ms, and error rates are 0%, so the symptom is pure latency amplification localized to the inventory catalog dependency.
diagnosis.recommended_fix: No code patch in pricing.py. Operationally: (a) remove/disable the injected `SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)` on the inventory-service catalog path and any fault flag driving it; (b) verify no scheduled job or sentinel artifact is issuing the sleep; (c) as hardening, either reduce the statement latency or raise the connection pool timeout in runtime.py above the statement time to avoid pool wait/timeout amplification; (d) monitor pg_stat_statements mean_exec_time for pg_sleep and inventory pool usage_ms to confirm recovery.
diagnosis.reasoning_summary: Three independent evidence types converge. (1) Postgres active-session list repeatedly shows inventory-service running `SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)`, and pg_stat_statements delta shows `SELECT pg_sleep($1)` with calls_delta=53 over 1s at mean_exec_time≈1202ms. (2) Distributed traces show the full ~1.21s of latency is the inventory-service /products client span (e.g. 1,211,765µs in trace 2cb20669...), while payment (~4ms) and user (~1ms) spans are negligible. (3) HTTP metrics show inventory-service p50≈1206ms with 0% errors and inventory pool usage_ms=93840 vs far lower peer values. Source review shows pricing.py (total price computation) has no catalog/DB/sleep logic and no `sleep` token exists in allowlisted files, so the fault is not in the patched module — it is an operational slow-query/sleep injection in the inventory path. The runtime pool timeout of 0.8s (runtime.py:24) is smaller than the 1.2s statement, making the pool vulnerable to waits under load.
remaining_uncertainty: Cannot inspect the fault harness/configuration (inaccessible), so the exact flag/toggle enabling pg_sleep is unconfirmed.
Whether the sleep is injected by the inventory app process or by an external control-plane artifact is not directly observable; the active-session application_name is inventory-service.
No long-window baseline was available to quantify exactly when the sleep began versus a pre-existing condition.

regression_risks: Raising the pool timeout above 1.2s (recommended hardening in the diagnosis) would mask the fault, allow stalled connections to accumulate, and could amplify latency under load if the sleep is ever removed while a long timeout remains; it may also degrade error propagation.

Removing/flagging the pg_sleep without addressing the underlying cache miss ratio (catalog TTL=30 and 85%+ misses) may leave residual DB load, and the fix's effectiveness cannot be validated without a before/after measurement.

Because the fault is operational and outside the allowlisted patch files, any patch attempt in pricing.py would be wrong; conversely, a no-code patch delivers no tested change, so 'recovery' cannot be claimed and the same injection could recur.

The 0.8s pool timeout vs 1.2s statement creates latent pool-timeout behavior; if the sleep is toggled off/on dynamically, the system may oscillate between healthy and saturated states, making SLO-based detection unreliable.

No rollback or post-change verification evidence exists, so if the sleep is externally reintroduced there is no guardrail or alert tied to pg_stat_statements mean_exec_time or inventory pool usage_ms.
critic.test_sufficiency: Insufficient. There is no controlled before/after measurement, no ablation that removes the sleep to confirm latency drops to baseline, and no negative control proving the sleep is causal rather than coincident. Evidence is observational and cumulative (operator signals, 20s metric window, 1s pg_stat_statements delta, sampled traces) with no long-window baseline, so timing of onset and confirmation of recovery are unestablished. The no-code-patch decision means no regression or acceptance test was run against a changed artifact; test coverage for the pricing contract (tests/pricing_contract.py) is unrelated to the inventory sleep. Verification of the diagnosis is limited to the observed scope and time window; production deployment and recovery are not demonstrated.
critic.verification_summary: Evidence strongly supports the diagnosis that an operational SELECT pg_sleep(1.2) on the inventory-service catalog path produces the ~1.2s latency: E-ca5f8aedbefa4af4 shows active sessions with application_name=inventory-service running 'SELECT pg_sleep(1.2)' and pg_stat_statements with 'SELECT pg_sleep($1)' mean_exec_time≈1202ms (calls_delta=53/s), E-599f949fc0174274 and E-709dc8606e294bcc show the inventory-service /products client span consuming ~1,212,033µs while sibling spans are milliseconds, and E-05d3a553906547d3 plus operator signals show ~1206ms inventory p50 with 0% errors. However, VERIFIED cannot be claimed because the exact injection mechanism, activation window, and recovery are not evidenced: there is no before/after measurement, no negative control, and no confirmation that a fault artifact is causing the sleep. The diagnosis is a coherent and well-supported inference, but not fully proven.
alternative_explanations: A separate scheduled job or sentinel/control-plane artifact (not the inventory application code) issues the pg_sleep against the same database; application_name=inventory-service could be set by a connection pool shared or reused by another process, or by a fault-injection harness that assumes that application_name.

Pool contention/saturation in inventory-service: usage_ms=93840 and requests_wait_ms=19 indicate the pool is heavily loaded with long-held connections; the 1.2s latency could be amplified by pool waits under max_size=4 and timeout=0.8s, meaning the sleep may be only one contributing factor rather than the sole cause.

Redis catalog caching: E-7b04a5ded28443b5 shows a very low keyspace hit ratio (29344 hits vs 177009 misses) and catalog_ttl=30; cache misses could force DB reads, and if the sleep is inside the DB path, misses and the sleep could interact, making the cache a second lever rather than the sleep being the sole root cause.

Downstream fan-out: order-service p50≈1232ms is higher than inventory p50≈1206ms, and order-service calls both inventory and payment; the observed end-to-end latency could partly reflect sequential fan-out or client timeout retries rather than a single inventory query, though trace E-709dc8606e294bcc pins the dominant span to the inventory client call.

Measurement/window ambiguity: E-05d3a553906547d3 covers only 20 seconds and the pg_stat_statements sample 1 second, so the sleep may be transient or coincident with the observation window rather than a standing condition.

diagnosis.hypothesis: inventory-service /products exhausts its 4-connection DB pool because each request executes a slow SELECT pg_sleep(2), holding connections beyond the 0.8s acquire timeout and producing PoolTimeout 500s that surface at the gateway as 502.
diagnosis.root_cause: The inventory-service /products path executes a blocking SELECT pg_sleep(2) against Postgres. Four inventory-service sessions are concurrently active on wait_event_type=Timeout / wait_event=PgSleep (E-e0f2290017c241aa), and pg_stat_statements shows the pg_sleep(2) variant with mean_exec_time ~2001.78 ms and a call delta of 47 during the sample window. Because the shared AsyncConnectionPool is configured with min_size=1, max_size=4, timeout=0.8s (services/runtime.py:24), each in-flight request holds a pooled connection for ~2s — far longer than the 0.8s acquire timeout. New requests therefore fail to acquire a connection and raise PoolTimeout, logged as inventory-service /products 500 'PoolTimeout: couldn't get a connection after 0.80 sec', which the gateway reports as /products 502 (E-a39dcebcec624568). Pool telemetry corroborates: inventory-service shows requests_queued=137, requests_wait_ms=80104 (cumulative ~80s waiting) and requests_errors=67 with the pool fully sized (pool_size=4, max_size=4), while other services remain healthy (E-f2a2bb7e87d344c7). The latency profile is consistent: inventory-service p50≈422ms, p95≈809ms with 48.4% errors, and gateway mirrors it at p50≈500ms, p95≈826ms, 48.4% errors (E-5b21ff94dcc44744). This is an injected slow-query/connection-holding fault, not a defect in the allowlisted pricing module: pricing.py contains only pure arithmetic and the contract tests pass against it; no pg_sleep or pool usage exists there.
diagnosis.recommended_fix: Operational only, outside pricing.py scope: stop/remove the injected slow query on inventory-service — the fault manifests as SELECT pg_sleep(2) on the /products path (likely gated by a fault flag keyed via redis 'fault:'+name, services/runtime.py:40-41). Terminate the offending sessions/variant, clear the fault flag, and restart or drain inventory-service to release held connections. As hardening (separate change, not this patch): separate read pools for slow paths, raise pool max_size, and shorten query statement_timeout so a single slow query cannot monopolize all 4 connections. Re-verify recovery by watching inventory-service pool requests_waiting/requests_errors return to 0 and gateway /products error rate fall to ~0%.
diagnosis.reasoning_summary: Two independent evidence types agree: (1) live Postgres activity/statements show inventory-service running SELECT pg_sleep(2) (~2001ms mean, 47 new calls) holding all 4 pool slots (E-e0f2290017c241aa); (2) inventory-service pool-stats show the pool saturated at max_size=4 with 137 queued requests, 80104ms cumulative wait, and 67 errors (E-f2a2bb7e87d344c7). Logs directly show the failure signature 'PoolTimeout: couldn't get a connection after 0.80 sec' on inventory /products 500 with gateway /products 502 (E-a39dcebcec624568), matching the pool timeout=0.8s in runtime.py:24 (E-d60c7dd7a36346c8). Metrics mirror the same 48.4% error and ~800ms p95 on inventory and gateway (E-5b21ff94dcc44744). The allowlisted pricing module is pure arithmetic (E-b6354fe343f0475f) with passing contract expectations (E-2bc061bbff7149a2) and no DB/pool code, so no code patch is warranted. Kafka lag is 0 and Redis/other services are healthy, excluding consumer lag and cache-miss causes.
remaining_uncertainty: The exact mechanism that injects the 2s sleep (fault flag vs. workload) is not directly observable; harness/truth is inaccessible.
Pool-stats figures are cumulative snapshots, so request-level distribution of waits could not be independently per-request confirmed.
No tracing span shows the sleep query directly inside the inventory request path (spans show Redis EXISTS/GET and the pg_sleep is only visible in DB activity/statements).

regression_risks: Recommended operational fix (raising pool max_size or adding statement_timeout) is outside the tested patch surface; changing pool size/timeout could shift contention to Postgres connection limits or other services sharing DSN.

Draining/restarting inventory-service to release connections may cause transient in-flight request loss and gateway 5xx spikes; no before/after measurement is provided to bound this (measured_before_after is null).

If the true cause is query volume or audit-path contention rather than an injected sleep, clearing only the hypothesized fault flag would not restore stability, producing an apparent non-fix and masking the real driver.

No code patch exists (patch: null); the 'allowlisted pricing module harmless' conclusion (E-b6354fe343f0475f, E-2bc061bbff7149a2) is a non-regression argument for a module unrelated to the failing path, so it provides weak assurance about the rest of the system.
Separating read pools or shortening statement_timeout could break the /checkout success path (currently 200s at ~480ms with /products ~403ms) by timing out legitimate queries.
critic.test_sufficiency: Insufficient for full verification. Evidence is consistent and multi-source, but the slow-query-to-pool-timeout causal chain is not directly instrumented: no trace span shows pg_sleep inside the failing inventory request path, the per-service attribution of the 47 pg_sleep call delta rests on application_name, and pool-stats are cumulative snapshots without per-request distribution. The 'injected' nature is unproven (repository searches for pg_sleep/fault returned no matches). Because this is NO_CODE_PATCH with identical before/after absence (measured_before_after null), no recovery or fix verification is possible; the diagnosis can at most be rated PARTIALLY_VERIFIED on mechanism plausibility, not on confirmed causality or remediation.
critic.verification_summary: The suppression chain is well supported by concordant evidence: (1) inspect_database (E-e0f2290017c241aa) shows four active inventory-service sessions blocked at wait_event_type=Timeout/PgSleep and a pg_sleep variant with mean_exec_time ~2001.78 ms whose call_delta=47 in-window; (2) pool-stats (E-f2a2bb7e87d344c7) show inventory-service saturated at pool_size=4/max=4 with requests_queued=137, requests_wait_ms=80104, requests_errors=67 while peer services are healthy; (3) search_logs (E-a39dcebcec624568) capture the exact failure signature 'PoolTimeout: couldn't get a connection after 0.80 sec' on inventory /products 500 paired with gateway /products 502; (4) runtime.py:24 (E-d60c7dd7a36346c8) sets max_size=4 and timeout=0.8s, mechanistically consistent with 2s connection holds starving acquirers; (5) query_metrics (E-5b21ff94dcc44744) mirror the 48.4% error rate and ~800ms p95 across inventory and gateway. However, the diagnosis is not fully verified: the slow-query-to-pool-timeout link is inferential rather than instrumented. No span in the supplied traces (E-858b8a9a4af34456, E-8dffc3a08bb543a9) shows the pg_sleep query executing inside the inventory request path; inventory GET /products spans show ~403-409ms duration with only Redis EXISTS/GET children, below the ~800-830ms failed-request durations. The 47 calls_delta attribution to inventory relies on application_name, not a per-query service breakdown, and pool-stats are cumulative snapshots (matching the diagnosis's own stated uncertainty). The 'injected fault' framing is unsupported: E-ef8ed4f1e8a14661 and E-49a6557209024ddd return zero matches for pg_sleep/pool/fault in the searched scope, so the injection mechanism (Redis 'fault:' flag per runtime.py:40-41) is not evidenced. Diagnostic verification does not imply recovery: this is NO_CODE_PATCH and no remediation was performed.
alternative_explanations: Pool starvation from query volume alone: the products listing query executes 331 calls at ~0.08ms; if concurrent /products volume transiently exceeds 4 slots, PoolTimeout could arise without a pg_sleep in the request path. E-e0f2290017c241aa pairs both the normal listing query and pg_sleep calls to inventory-service, so causality is not isolated.

Pool misconfiguration as sufficient cause: timeout=0.8s against a workload where legitimately slow queries approach ~0.8s means any moderately slow query (even one near the p95 of 809ms) can trip acquire failures; the fault could be latency amplification rather than an injected sleep.

Audit-path contention: runtime.py routes request_logs inserts through a separate audit_pool (max_size=2); under high error volume the audit writes could themselves queue, though E-a39dcebcec624568 shows successful 200 request_logs, weakening this alternative for the observed failures.

Redis fault-flag evaluation: each request path may call redis.exists('fault:'+name) (runtime.py:40-41) and the span evidence (E-8dffc3a08bb543a9) shows Redis EXISTS/GET calls in the inventory path; if Redis latency or flag toggling interacts with request handling, some latency could originate there rather than only in Postgres.

Gateway-level 502 origin: the gateway could be enforcing its own upstream timeout and emitting 502 independently of inventory's specific PoolTimeout, meaning the gateway symptom may be partially decoupled from the pool mechanism.

judgment.explanation: The diagnosis matches the ground truth: inventory-service's 4-slot DB pool is exhausted by concurrent long-running queries holding connections. Evidence independently corroborates both required observations: pg activity shows active 'SELECT pg_sleep(2)' sessions on inventory-service (E-e0f2290017c241aa), and inventory pool-stats show pool saturated at max_size=4 with 137 queued requests and 67 errors (E-f2a2bb7e87d344c7), plus PoolTimeout logs and mirrored 48.4% error metrics (E-a39dcebcec624568, E-5b21ff94dcc44744). The causal mechanism—long queries held beyond the 0.8s acquire timeout producing PoolTimeout/502—is materially correct; the pg_sleep injection detail is an acceptable higher-level mechanism. Two independent supporting observations yield evidence quality 2.

diagnosis.hypothesis: inventory-service's GET /products performs an N+1 per-row fan-out of single-row SELECTs over a small connection pool (max_size=4, timeout=0.8s), causing connection-checkout contention that inflates inventory latency and, transitively, gateway latency — with zero HTTP errors.
diagnosis.root_cause: inventory-service retrieves product rows with one single-row query per item instead of a set-based query (N+1). The distributed trace b5e9a1213aca8862cd05d6a03a4be69e shows many repeated 'SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products WHERE id=%s' spans (each ~20µs) inside a single GET /products request, and pg_stat_statements reports that same single-row SELECT was called 15,360 times while list queries (SELECT id ... ORDER BY id LIMIT) were issued only 377–384 times — i.e. ~40 single-row queries per list request. Each query is individually fast (mean exec ~0.04ms), but the volume per request multiplied by concurrency saturates inventory's connection pool (pool_max=4, timeout=0.8s in services/runtime.py line 24). Pool stats confirm checkout starvation: requests_queued=230, requests_wait_ms=135851, requests_errors=114, pool_size=pool_max=4, while every other service shows ~0 queueing. The resulting inventory p95 ~119ms/p99 ~161ms propagates to gateway (p95 ~188ms), matching the observed signal fan-out, with 0% HTTP errors because the contention manifests as latency, not exceptions.
diagnosis.recommended_fix: Replace the per-row product lookup loop in inventory-service with a single set-based query (e.g. SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products WHERE id = ANY($1) or a single ordered list query) to eliminate the N+1, and/or raise the connection pool size for inventory-service. The N+1 implementation is not in the allowlisted source files (only services/pricing.py, services/runtime.py, tests/pricing_contract.py are readable) and runtime.py is shared generic infrastructure, so no in-scope code patch is safe here. Operational recommendation: rewrite the inventory /products handler to fetch all products in one query; as a mitigation, increase pool max_size and consider caching the product catalog (Redis keyspace_misses 189,416 vs hits 32,258 suggests low cache effectiveness).
diagnosis.reasoning_summary: Three independent evidence types agree. (1) Traces: single GET /products trace contains repeated per-row products SELECT spans (~20µs each), evidencing per-row fan-out. (2) Database: pg_stat_statements shows the single-row products SELECT called 15,360 times vs only ~380 list queries (~40x per request), all with mean exec ~0.04ms — queries are healthy, so volume is the issue. (3) Pool stats: inventory-service is the only service with heavy checkout contention (requests_queued 230, requests_wait_ms 135851ms, requests_errors 114, pool_size=pool_max=4). (4) HTTP metrics: inventory p95 119ms and gateway p95 188ms dominate, with 0% errors — the latency-only signature of pool contention behind an N+1. The pool is configured in runtime.py (max_size=4, timeout=0.8s).
remaining_uncertainty: The exact inventory-service source implementing the per-row loop is not in the allowlisted repository files, so the N+1 cannot be cited at a file/line; the fan-out is inferred from traces and pg_stat_statements.
Redis keyspace_misses are cumulative and include control-plane traffic, so cache effectiveness for the catalog cannot be precisely quantified.
Cumulative pool counters (requests_num, usage_ms) are totals; only requests_queued/requests_wait_ms/requests_errors relative magnitudes were used to localize contention.

regression_risks: No patch was applied (NO_CODE_PATCH); recommended and in-code changes (rewrite to set-based query, raise pool max_size, add caching) carry unvalidated regression risk because they are untested here.

Changing the shared services/runtime.py pool configuration (max_size, timeout) affects ALL services, not just inventory; raising max_size could increase DB load and introduce connection exhaustion; lowering/waiting could worsen other services.

Replacing the per-row SELECT with ANY($1)/set-based query changes SQL semantics (ordering, parameter handling, response shape) and could break callers if row ordering or per-row error handling is relied upon.

Adding Redis caching could mask the N+1 without fixing it and could serve stale inventory (price/stock), creating correctness risk for stock-dependent operations (e.g., checkout), especially with a 30s TTL.
The allowlisted pricing.py / tests changes cannot address inventory at all, so any applied patch in allowlisted scope would be a no-op with respect to this diagnosis; no causal link is closed.
Because the pool stats used are cumulative, a fix evaluated only against cumulative deltas could give a false positive/negative; per-request measurement is needed and is absent.
critic.test_sufficiency: INSUFFICIENT. Supporting evidence is observational and inferential: trace fan-out and pg_stat_statements call ratios strongly corroborate N+1, and pool stats localize contention to inventory. But (a) the handler code implementing the loop is not in the allowlisted source, so the mechanism is not directly observed; (b) there is no controlled experiment, no direct measurement of per-request pool wait time, no before/after comparison, and no A/B test isolating the loop from pool size or being the sole cause; (c) counter evidence is cumulative (pg_stat_statements, pool requests_num/usage_ms, Redis keyspace) rather than time-windowed; (d) no falsification test distinguishes N+1 from a shared connection/DSN or pg_sleep bottleneck. The diagnosis is plausible and best-supported but not decisively proven, and no production recovery or deployment is claimed.
critic.verification_summary: The N+1 mechanism and pool-contention localization are supported by converging trace and DB evidence. E-0767127f3e354628 shows a single GET /products trace (b5e9a1213aca8862cd05d6a03a4be69e) containing repeated 'SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products WHERE id=%s' spans of ~20 microseconds each, consistent with per-row fan-out. E-413a0bb36f214b41 reports the identical single-row SELECT called 15,360 times vs only 377-384 list queries (~40x), with mean exec ~0.04ms, and shows the same query resident in pg_stat_activity under inventory-service. E-cfadc1f753a74f2a shows inventory-service is the only service with material checkout contention (requests_queued=230, requests_wait_ms=135851, requests_errors=114, pool_size=pool_max=4) while peers show ~1-2 queued and ~0-2ms wait. HTTP metrics (E-677f476162374132) show inventory p95 ~119ms/p99 ~161ms and gateway p95 ~188ms with 0% errors, matching a latency-only contention signature. However, the causal chain is not fully closed: the specific handler code implementing the per-row loop is not in the allowlisted source (E-e79b7e217bb8470a, E-4e2eee3b5d244872), so only inferred; the pool configuration cited (services/runtime.py line 24, pool max_size=4/timeout=0.8s) is shared generic infrastructure (E-bb01c1e22b4245b7) that is used by all services, not inventory-specific; the actual pool counters attributed to inventory are cumulative totals (min_size=1/max_size=4 defaults apply uniformly), and per-request latency attribution is inferred rather than directly measured; and Redis cumulative stats (E-cc67a1c958ce40f9) are inconclusive. The diagnosis (N+1 plus pool contention) is well supported as the dominant explanation, but VERIFIED is withheld because the code-level root cause is not directly observed and no patch was applied or tested. This is a NO_CODE_PATCH diagnosis, so verification does not imply recovery.
alternative_explanations: Independent pool starvation caused by a slow consumer or a separate long-held connection path (e.g., another inventory route or background task holding connections), rather than N+1 fan-out; the presence of requests_errors=114 indicates some queries timed out after 0.8s, which individually exceed the ~0.04ms exec time and suggest queuing/blocking beyond simple per-query volume.

The pg_stat_statements call counts are cumulative and may include historical traffic unrelated to the incident window; the ~40x ratio could be a persistent workload artifact rather than the cause of the observed latency, and could coexist with a different transient bottleneck.

The pool stats are per-service cumulative counters scraped once; inventory's higher requests_num (16186) and usage_ms (488346) partly reflect higher request volume, so 'contention' could be a function of traffic scaling rather than a code defect, especially since all services share the same max_size=4 default.

Cache effect: with catalog TTL 30s and high cumulative keyspace_misses, cache misses could drive repeated DB lookups independent of N+1 structure.

judgment.explanation: The diagnosis correctly identifies an N+1 pattern in inventory-service: the get_trace evidence shows repeated single-row 'SELECT id,name,price,stock FROM products WHERE id=%s' spans within a single GET /products request, and inspect_database shows that exact single-row query as inventory-service's active statement, consistent with per-product SELECTs (~40 per request). This matches the ground-truth root cause (one ID query followed by forty per-product SELECT statements) and the affected service (inventory-service). It differs only in attributing the latency to pool-contention amplification rather than the raw query count, a plausible downstream mechanism that does not contradict the core N+1 cause. Evidence quality is 2: two independent supporting observations (distributed traces showing repeated per-row SELECT spans, and database/pool statistics localizing the fan-out to inventory-service without errors).

diagnosis.hypothesis: inventory-service experience cache-miss / DB-read amplification: a 4s catalog TTL plus per-request fault-check round trips produce repeated product lookups, inflating downstream fan-out latency at gateway/order-service without any HTTP errors.
diagnosis.root_cause: No error condition (0% errors on every service) and all services report healthy, so this is a latency/throughput degradation, not an exception. The dominant measured anomaly is inventory-service pool contention: 26,873 cumulative requests with 230 queued and 135,851 ms cumulative request wait plus 114 request errors, far out of line with its tiny ~3.5 ms HTTP latency (E-3b88de98c6224beb). DB statement stats (E-32f0adb737494976) show product lookups are the highest-volume statement (25,040 calls, ~0.039 ms mean) and the two pg_sleep rows (176 calls @ ~2002 ms, 159 calls @ ~1202 ms) are separate slow-statement noise, not the product path. Redis (E-f0c67c5515884b5a) reports keyspace_misses 205,339 vs hits 35,275 with a catalog TTL of only 4 s, so a 4 s TTL is shorter than the request cadence and forces repeated re-reads of the product catalog. Traces (E-55f25a18e2504730, E-afb2ed88281e479c) show repeated Redis EXISTS spans (the fault() helper) fanning out per request alongside fast DB writes, consistent with per-request Redis round trips rather than backend slowness. Gateway p95 ~57-62 ms and order-service p95 ~39-43 ms (E-2d1d615b89d34794) are consistent with accumulated downstream fan-out latency on the checkout/products path with no failures. The evidence supports cache-miss/read amplification as the category; a pure DATABASE_SLOW_QUERY is not supported because per-call DB exec times are sub-millisecond and pg_sleep calls are a disjoint statement.
diagnosis.recommended_fix: Operationally raise the product catalog TTL well above the product request cadence, batch/eliminate the per-request Redis EXISTS fault() check, and validate cache-hit ratio recovery. Because the caching logic is not present in the allowlisted pricing.py scope, and the closest code (runtime.py pool/fault helper) is infrastructure configuration rather than an in-scope defect, apply NO_CODE_PATCH and hand off an operational recommendation to increase catalog TTL and reduce per-request Redis round trips. Stopping the experiment is not a code fix.
diagnosis.reasoning_summary: Two independent evidence types agree: (1) live pool-stats show inventory-service as the sole outlier in queued requests (230) and cumulative wait (135851 ms) with 114 request errors despite ~3.5 ms HTTP latency; (2) Redis counters show miss-dominated access with a 4 s catalog TTL, and traces show repeated Redis EXISTS round trips per request. DB per-call exec times for product lookups are sub-millisecond, ruling out a genuinely slow query as the driver. With zero HTTP errors across services, the symptom is latency/read amplification from short cache TTL plus per-request Redis checks, not an exception. The only inspectable sources (pricing.py, runtime.py, tests/pricing_contract.py) contain no product-cache or TTL logic; runtime.py's fault() helper and pool configuration are the closest related code.
remaining_uncertainty: Product catalog cache/TTL logic source is not in the allowlisted files, so the exact miss cause cannot be confirmed by reading code.
pg_sleep statements (2s and 1.2s mean) are unresolved injection noise; their origin is outside the inspectable source and could contribute to DB load.
Whether the 4s TTL is the sole driver versus the per-request fault() EXISTS round trips cannot be separated without the inventory code.
The 114 inventory request errors are not visible in HTTP logs (0% error), so their exact nature is unconfirmed.

regression_risks: Raising catalog TTL may delay product/stock visibility; inventory stock changes could be served stale, affecting order correctness.
Removing or batching the per-request Redis EXISTS fault() check changes fault-injection control-plane semantics and could disable intended fault behavior in tests or chaos runs.
Increasing pool_max to relieve queuing may overload Postgres connections, especially while disjoint pg_sleep statements consume DB capacity.
Operational TTL/round-trip changes are untested in the supplied evidence; no before/after measurement exists (patch is null, measured_before_after null), so any change is unverified.
Treating latency as benign (0% errors) risks masking the 114 inventory request_errors, whose nature is unconfirmed.
critic.test_sufficiency: Insufficient. The diagnosis rests on correlational, cumulative, and disjoint-time-window evidence. Pool stats (E-3b88de98c6224beb) and Redis counters (E-f0c67c5515884b5a) are cumulative snapshot values without a baseline or delta; keyspace_misses explicitly includes control-plane traffic. The Redis snapshot shows no per-key or product-catalog hit/miss breakdown, so the TTL->miss->re-read causal link is untested. HTTP metrics (E-2d1d615b89d34794, E-08a831ab586248ef) show ~154-232 requests, which dilutes significance of tail numbers. Critically, the 114 inventory request_errors are not cross-checked against application logs (0% HTTP errors) and remain unexplained. No controlled test compares TTL/fault() behavior with latency, and no patch or before/after measurement exists to confirm the recommended intervention would recover cache-hit ratio or reduce fan-out latency.
critic.verification_summary: The evidence supports a latency-only degradation with no HTTP errors (E-2d1d615b89d34794, E-08a831ab586248ef: 0.00% errors, all 200s), and inventory-service pool stats are the only real outlier (E-3b88de98c6224beb: requests_queued 230, requests_wait_ms 135851, requests_num 26873, requests_errors 114). Redis counters are miss-dominated (E-f0c67c5515884b5a: misses 205339 vs hits 35275) with catalog_ttl=4, and traces show repeated per-request Redis EXISTS spans (E-55f25a18e2504730, E-afb2ed88281e479c). DB per-call exec for product lookups is sub-millisecond (E-32f0adb737494976: 0.039ms), consistent with the claim that a slow-query cause is unsupported. However, the diagnosis is only partially verified: the specific causal chain (4s TTL -> cache misses -> inflated gateway/order latency) is asserted rather than demonstrated. No key-level cache instrumentation proves product-catalog misses drive re-reads; keyspace_misses is cumulative and the evidence itself notes it includes control-plane traffic; runtime.py fault() checks 'fault:*' keys, not catalog keys (E-a5cc57fce6e243b4, E-8f77f0866f474748), so existing trace spans do not show catalog re-reads. Simple arithmetic also creates tension: 26873 pool requests at ~7.8 rps over ~57 min is plausible, but ~135851ms wait / 26873 requests (~5ms/req average) does not obviously explain 30-60ms gateway/order p95s without a demonstrated per-request fan-out multiplier. The diagnosis appropriately concedes uncertainty (allowlisted source absent, pg_sleep unresolved, TTL vs fault() inseparability, 114 errors not visible in HTTP logs). The recommended NO_CODE_PATCH boundary is correct because no patchable caching/TTL code exists in scope (E-8c62df3e1bc74c90, E-a71b77dcc27d41f7, E-7995d69209524806, E-8f77f0866f474748).
alternative_explanations: Connection-pool saturation alone (pool_max=4, timeout=0.8s) rather than cache-miss amplification could produce queued requests and wait_ms; the two are not separated by the supplied evidence.

Postgres contention/noise from the disjoint pg_sleep statements (E-32f0adb737494976: 176 @ ~2002ms, 159 @ ~1202ms; call_delta 17 in one sample) could intermittently load the DB and inflate wait, consistent with the 114 pool request_errors that are absent from HTTP logs.

Unbounded per-request Redis EXISTS calls from the fault() helper (E-a5cc57fce6e243b4, E-8f77f0866f474748) may be the dominant Redis round-trip cost, independent of the 4s TTL; the diagnosis itself lists this as inseparable.
A client/load-driver-side cadence (repeated /products re-reads at ~2.2-4.9ms each, E-1cab8850e1354474) could inflate fan-out without Redis catalog misses being the driver.
Kafka consumer lag (E-2f11fbe5614b4567: lag 160) could indicate asynchronous backpressure contributing to latency, though it is not connected to this request path in the evidence.

judgment.explanation: The ground truth root cause is Kafka consumer lag on notification-service: the notification consumer pauses processing and commits, so end offsets grow while committed offsets stay fixed (recovery: resume consumer and drain backlog). The submitted diagnosis instead claims a CACHE_MISS / read-amplification mechanism in inventory-service driven by a 4s catalog TTL and per-request Redis EXISTS fault checks. This is a materially different category, service, and causal mechanism, and it directly contradicts the ground truth. Critically, the injected Kafka lag evidence is present in the environment payload (inspect_kafka shows lag=160 with end_offset=10144 and committed_offset=9984) yet the diagnosis completely ignores it. The 'EXISTS' Redis spans the diagnosis relies on are the fault-injection helper (fault()/redis.exists), not evidence of a legitimate cache-miss root cause, so the proposed mechanism mischaracterizes injection infrastructure as the root cause. The diagnosis is wrong on category, affected service, and mechanism, so no credit is warranted despite citing some evidence.
